label: lem:BMalgP
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:BMalgP}
 Let $X$ be an oriented graph whose adjacency matrix $A$ belongs to the Bose-Mesner algebra of $\mathcal{A}$.  
 If PST occurs from $a$ to $b$ where $a\neq b$ at time $\tau$, then $U(\tau) \in \mathcal{A}$ is the permutation 
 matrix of a fixed-point-free automorphism of $X$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First observe that $U(t) \in \mathrm{span}\ \mathcal{A}$, for any time $t$. If PST occurs from $a$ to $b$ at time $\tau$ then the $(b,a)$-entry is the only non-zero entry in column $a$ of $U(\tau)$.
    We see the $U(\tau) = \lambda A_j$ for some $A_j \in \mathcal{A}$ with $k_j=1$.  Since $(A_j)_{a,a}=0$, $j\neq 0$ and $A_j$ is a fixed-point-free permutation.  

    Now $A$ is a sum of matrices of the form $A_i - A_i^T$.  Since $A_iJ=A_i^TJ$, the vector of all ones ${\bf 1}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ with eigenvalue $0$.
    Whence
    \begin{equation*}
      \lambda {\bf 1} =  \lambda A_j {\bf 1} = U(\tau) {\bf 1}= e^{0\tau} {\bf 1},
    \end{equation*}
    and $\lambda=1$. 
    Since $A_j$ commutes with $A$, $A_j$ is the permutation matrix of an automorphism of $X$.
head: environment

label: thm:BMalgCyclicP
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:BMalgCyclicP}
    Let $X$ be an oriented graph with adjacency matrix $A$ belongs to the Bose-Mesner algebra of some association scheme $\mathcal{A}$.
    Let $\tau>0$ be the smallest time at which PST occurs from $a$ to another vertex in $X$.
    Then, the following statements hold.
    \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
    	\item $U(\tau)$ is an automorphism of $X$ that acts cyclically on $\mathcal{S}_a$. 
    	\item The matrix $U(\tau)$ has order $|\mathcal{S}_a|$.
    	\item For any two vertices $a,b\in V(X)$ such that $a \not\equiv b$, we have $|\mathcal{S}_a| = |\mathcal{S}_b|$
    \end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

label: cor:BMalgSize
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $A=\sum_{r} \theta_r E_r$ be the spectral decomposition of $A$.  
Since $A\in \mathrm{span}\ \mathcal{A}$, the eigenvalue support of $a$, $\Phi_a$, contains all eigenvalues of $A$.
By Theorem~6.1 of \cite{godsil2020perfect}, there exists a square-free positive integer $\Delta$ such that $\Phi_a \subset {\mathbb{Z}}(i\sqrt{\Delta})$.

From Theorem~\ref{thm:BMalgCyclicP}, $U(\tau)=P$ is a permutation matrix of order $m=\vert \mathcal{S}_a\vert$.  For $r=0,\ldots,d$, $ PE_r = \omega_r E_r$ for some $m$-th root of unity $\omega_r$.  Since $P$ is a permutation matrix, it follows from \cite[Lemma~2.10.3]{lato2019quantum}  that $\omega_r \in \mathbb{Q}(i\sqrt{\Delta})$.  Hence $m \in \{2,3,4,6\}$.

{
Suppose $m\in \{3, 6\}$.  There exists $r$ such that $\omega_r$ is a primitive $m$-th root of unity, so $\Delta=3$.
It follows from $PE_r = \omega_rE_r$ and Theorem~2.10.3 of \cite{lato2019quantum} that $\sqrt{3}i \in \mathbb{Q}(\theta_r)$.  Hence $\theta_r \in \sqrt{3}i \mathbb{Z}$, and $\tau \in \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{3}} \mathbb{Q}$
by Corollary~6.1.3 of \cite{lato2019quantum}.

Similarly, when $m=4$, there exists $r$ such that $PE_r = i E_r$ which implies $i\in \mathbb{Q}(\theta_r)$.
Thus $\theta_r \in i\mathbb{Z}$ and $\tau \in \pi\mathbb{Q}$.
}
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Let $X$ be an oriented graph whose adjacency matrix $A$ belongs to the Bose-Mesner algebra of some association scheme $\mathcal{A}$.
    If PST occurs in $X$ at time $\tau$ then there exist $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_s$ such that $V(X)$ is the disjoint union of $\mathcal{S}_{a_1},\cdots, \mathcal{S}_{a_s}$, and $\vert \mathcal{S}_{a_j} \vert = \vert V(X)\vert /s$, for $j=1,\ldots,s$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $m$ be the order of the permutation matrix $P=U(\tau)$ as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:BMalgCyclicP}.  Since $P \in \mathcal{A}$, up to re-ordering of vertices, $P$ is a block diagonal matrix in which every block is a $m\times m$ permutation matrix of order $m$.   Let $a_j$ be a vertex in the $j$-th block and the result follows.
head: environment

label: thm:cayleysatset
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:cayleysatset}
    If $\mathrm{Cay}(G, C)$ is an oriented normal Cayley graph admitting PST, then $\mathcal{S}_e$ is a cyclic subgroup of $Z(G)$ that has order $2$, $3$, $4$, or $6$.
head: environment

label: lem:PSTequiv
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:PSTequiv}
In an oriented normal Cayley graph,
PST occurs from $a$ to $b$ at time $\tau$ if and only if PST occurs from $e$ to $ba^{-1}$.
Further, $ba^{-1}$ is a central element of $G$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $P$ be the permutation matrix of the automorphism of $X$ that maps $g$ to $ga^{-1}$.
Then $PU(\tau)=U(\tau)P$, and $U(\tau)a=b$ if and only if $U(\tau)e=ba^{-1}$.  
By Theorem~\ref{thm:BMalgCyclicP}, $ba^{-1} \in \mathcal{S}_e \subset Z(G)$.

label: thm:solvableMST
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:solvableMST}
    If $G$ is a solvable group, $\mathrm{Cay}(G, C)$ is an oriented normal Cayley graph admitting PST, then $\mathcal{S}_e$ is a cyclic subgroup of $Z(G)$ that has order either $2$, or $3$, or $4$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume the contrary. Then, by Theorem~\ref{thm:cayleysatset}, there is a
  solvable group $G$ of order $6n$ and $C \subset G$ such that $\mathrm{Cay}(G, C)$ is an oriented normal Cayley graph, with $\mathcal{S}_{e}$ equal to a cyclic subgroup $Z$  of order $6$ in $Z(G)$.

  We shall apply the theory of $p$-special characters, as developed (in far greater generality) in \cite{Gajendragadkar}, for the primes $p=2$ and $3$. For this purpose we recall some definitions. Given a character $\phi$ of a group $H$, we define
  $\det(\phi)(h)$ to be the determinant of $T(h)$, where $T$ is
  any matrix representation affording $\phi$. This is a well-defined linear character of $H$.  Let $p$ be a prime. An irreducible
  character $\chi$ is {\it $p$-special} if $\chi(1)$ is a power of $p$
  and the following further conditions hold: for every subnormal subgroup
  $H$ of $G$ and every irreducible constituent $\phi$ of $\chi_H$,
  the order of $\det(\phi)$ is a power of $p$.

  Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be characters of $Z$ of order $2$ and $3$
  respectively, By \cite[Cor. 4.8]{Gajendragadkar}, $G$ has a $2$-special
  irreducible character $\chi$ such that $\chi_Z$ is a multiple of $\alpha$.
  Likewise, $G$ has a $3$-special irreducible character $\psi$ such that
  $\psi_Z$ is a multiple of $\beta$. Hence
  by Condition~(\ref{Cond:chi}) in Theorem~\ref{thm:characterization} we have $\theta_\chi\neq 0$ and $\theta_\psi\neq 0$.
  
  By \cite[Prop. 6.3(a)]{Gajendragadkar},  $\mathbb Q(\chi)$ lies in
  a cyclotomic field of order equal to the  $2$-power in the exponent of $G$,
  and $\mathbb Q(\psi)$ lies in
  a cyclotomic field of order equal to the  $3$-power in the exponent of $G$. The intersection of these
  cyclotomic fields is $\mathbb Q$. Hence Corollary~\ref{cor:non-exist} applies.

label: thm:NoOrder4
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:NoOrder4}

    An oriented Cayley graph on $\mathbb{Z}_4^n$ does not have MST on a set of size 4.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $\langle z\rangle$ be a cyclic subgroup of order $4$. Let $\lambda$ be the character of $\langle z\rangle$ such that $\lambda(z)=-1$. There is a subgroup $A$ with ${\mathbb Z_4}^n=\langle z\rangle\times A$. Thus, $\lambda$ can be extended to a character of ${\mathbb Z_4}^n$  whose values are rational. The result now follows Corollary~\ref{cor:non-exist}.
head: environment

label: lem:nonlin
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:nonlin}
 Given a non-linear character $ \chi \in \mathrm{Irr}(M_{2}(n))$, then (i) $\chi(g)=0$, for all $g \notin Z(M_{2}(n))$; and (ii) $\chi(x^{2^{n-3}})=\pm 2i$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Clifford theory (\cite[Corollary~6.19]{isaacs1994character}, since $[M_{2}(n): \langle x\rangle]=2$, given any non-linear irreducible character $\chi$, its restriction $\chi|_{\langle x \rangle}$ is a sum of distinct conjugates of a linear character of $\psi \in \mathrm{Irr}(\langle x \rangle)$. The set of conjugates of $\psi$ is $\{\psi,\ \psi^{\sigma}\}$ and thus $\chi|_{\langle x \rangle}=\psi +\psi^{\sigma}$. Since $\psi \neq \psi^{\sigma}$, we must have $o(\psi)= 2^{n-1}$. Thus, $\psi(x)$ must be a primitive $2^{n-1}$th root of unity. Therefore, (ii) follows from the fact that $\chi|_{\langle x \rangle}=\psi +\psi^{\sigma}$.

 Given a non-central element $g$, let $h \in M_{2}(n)$ be such that $hgh^{-1}g^{-1} \neq e$. Since $\{e,\ x^{2^{n-2}}\}$ is the commutator, it follows that $hgh^{-1}g^{-1}=x^{2^{n-2}}$, and thus $hgh^{-1}=x^{2^{n-2}}g$. Therefore, 
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:noncentral}
 \chi(g)=\chi(hgh^{-1})=\chi(x^{2^{n-2}}g) =\dfrac{\chi(x^{2^{n-2}})}{\chi(e)} \chi(g),
 \end{equation}
 with the last equality following from the fact that $x^{2^{n-2}}$ is a central element. As $x^{2^{n-2}}$ is an element of order $2$ and $\psi$ is faithful, it follows that $\psi(x^{2^{n-2}})=-1$, and thus $\chi(x^{2^{n-2}})=-2$. Using \eqref{eq:noncentral}, it follows that
 $\chi(g)=-\chi(g)$, and thus (i) is true.

label: thm:mm-c
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:mm-c}
 Let $n\geq 5$, \[M_{2}(n) =\left\langle x,\sigma\ \lvert \ x^{2^{n-1}}=\sigma^2=e,\ \sigma x \sigma =x^{2^{n-2}+1} \right\rangle, \]
and let 
\[ C= \{x^{2^{n-3}},\ x^{2^{n-4}}\sigma,\ x^{2^{n-2}+2^{n-4}}\sigma \} \bigcup \{x^{4k+1}\ :\ 0\leq k \leq 2^{n-3}-1 \}\]
 Then $\mathrm{Cay}(M_{2}(n), C)$ is an oriented normal Cayley graph on $M_{2}(n)$, which admits MST on $\left\langle x^{2^{n-3}} \right\rangle$.

label: lem:centralcharacterc2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:centralcharacterc2}
Let $f:[n]\to \mathrm{Irr}(G)$ be a function, let  $\Lambda$ a partition-valued function on $\mathrm{Irr}(G)$ satisfying $|\Lambda(\phi)|=|f^{-1}(\phi)|$, for all $\phi \in \mathrm{Irr}(G)$, and let $\pi \in S_{n}$ be an $n$-cycle.
Then the following statements are true for all $\mathbf{x}\in G^{n}$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item If $|f([n])|>1$, then 
    \[\dfrac{\psi_{f,\Lambda}((\mathbf{x}; \pi)-\overline{\psi_{f,\Lambda}((\mathbf{x}; \pi)}}{\psi_{f,\Lambda}(1)}=0;\] and
    \item if $f([n])=\{\phi\}$, then 
    \[
    |G|^{n-1} \times\dfrac{\psi_{f,\Lambda}((\mathbf{x}; \pi)-\overline{\psi_{f,\Lambda}((\mathbf{x}; \pi)}}{\psi_{f,\Lambda}(1)} = k_{f,\Lambda}|Z(G)|^{(n-1)} \dfrac{\phi\left( \mathbf{x}_{\pi}  \right)-\overline{\phi\left( \mathbf{x}_{\pi}  \right)}}{\phi(1) \times (n-1)!},
    \]
    for some $k_{f,\Lambda} \in \mathbb{Z}$. 
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We recall from the definition \eqref{eq:charwreathproduct} that $\psi_{f,\Lambda}$ is a character induced from the subgroup $G\wr S_{\mathcal{B}_{f}}$, where $S_{\mathcal{B}_{f}}$ is the subgroup of $S_{n}$ preserving the partition $\mathcal{B}_{f}=\{f^{-1}(\mu)\ : \mu \in \mathrm{Irr}(G)\}$ of $[n]$. We note that $S_{\mathcal{B}_{f}}$ contains an $n$-cycle if and only if $|f([n])|=1$. Therefore, in case $|f([n])|>1$, no element of $G \wr S_{n}$ is conjugate to $(\mathbf{x}; \pi)$. Now, the Frobenius formula for induced characters implies part (1).

We now assume that $f([n])=\{\phi\}$. In this case, we have $S_{\mathcal{B}_{f}}=S_{n}$; $\lambda:=\Lambda(\phi) \vdash n$ and $\Lambda(\mu)=[0]$, for all $\mu \in \mathrm{Irr}(G)\setminus \{\phi\}$; and $\psi_{f,\Lambda}= \widetilde{\phi^{n}_{\lambda}}$. Using the well-known formula (see \cite[Lemma 4.3.9]{James_1984} or \cite[$(8.2)$, Appendix B]{macdonald1998symmetric}) for values of $\widetilde{\phi^{n}_{\lambda}}$, we have 
\begin{align*}
   |G|^{n-1}\times \dfrac{\psi_{f,\Lambda}((\mathbf{x}; \pi)-\overline{\psi_{f,\Lambda}((\mathbf{x}; \pi)}}{\psi_{f,\Lambda}(1) } & = |G|^{n-1} \times \dfrac{\rho_{\lambda}(\pi)\phi(\mathbf{x}_{\pi})-\overline{\rho_{\lambda}(\pi)\phi(\mathbf{x}_{\pi})}}{\phi^{n}(1) \rho_{\lambda}(1)}\\
    &= \dfrac{\rho_{\lambda}(\pi)}{\rho_{\lambda}(1)} \times\dfrac{|G|^{n-1}}{\phi^{n}(1)} \dfrac{\phi(\mathbf{x}_{\pi})-\overline{\phi(\mathbf{x}_{\pi})}}{\phi(1) }. 
\end{align*} 
 It is well known that $\frac{|G|}{\phi(1)} \equiv 0 \pmod{|Z(G)|}$. (see \cite[3.12]{isaacs1994character}). There are exactly $(n-1)!$ number of $n$-cycles in $S_{n}$. Using a well-known result \cite[Theorem 3.7]{isaacs1994character} on integrality of character values and the fact that irreducible characters of $S_{n}$ take on integer values, it follows that $\dfrac{\rho_{\lambda}(\pi)\times (n-1)!}{\rho_{\lambda}(1)}$ is an integer. Thus, the quantity $k_{f,\Lambda}= \dfrac{|G|^{n-1}}{\phi^{n-1}(1) |Z(G)|^{n-1}} \times \dfrac{\rho_{\lambda}(\pi)\times (n-1)!}{{\rho_{\lambda}(1)}}$. This concludes the proof of part (2).

title: Remark
body_md:
Recall that in \S~\ref{sec:nonsolvable}, we constructed connected oriented normal Cayley graphs on nonsolvable groups, which admit MST on sets of size $3$. It is natural to ask if there are ``nonsolvable'' examples in the case of MST on sets of size $4$. Theorem~\ref{thm:wreath} helps us construct infinitely many such examples. Let $G$, $\mathcal{C}$, $\tilde{C}_{1}$, and $\tilde{C}_{2}$ be as in Theorem~\ref{thm:wreath}. We recall the well-known fact that $\mathrm{Cay}(G, \mathcal{C})$ has as many (strongly) connected components as the index $[G : \left\langle C \right\rangle]$, with each component being isomorphic to $\mathrm{Cay}(\left\langle C \right\rangle,\ C)$. Assume that $C$ generates $G$. We note that $\tilde{C}_{1}$ generates $G^{n}$. We recall the fact that $n$-cycles in $S_{n}$ generate $S_{n}$ when $n$ is even and $A_{n}$ when $n$ is odd. Therefore, the subgroup $\left\langle \tilde{C}_{1} \cup \tilde{C_{2}} \right\rangle$ is $G\wr S_{n}$ when $n$ is even and $G\wr A_{n}$, when $n$ is odd. 
As $A_{n}$ is a nonabelian simple group when $n\geq 5$, both $G\wr S_{n}$ and $G \wr A_{n}$ are nonsolvable for $n\geq 5$. Theorem~\ref{thm:wreath} allows us to construct examples of MST of size 4 in connected oriented normal Cayley graphs of nonsolvable groups. For example, if $X$ is one of the examples in \cite[10.2]{GodsilZhan} which exhibits MST of size 4, then $X\wr 6$, is a connected oriented normal Cayley graph on a group with $S_{6}$ as one of its composition factors. Theorem~\ref{thm:wreath} asserts that $X \wr 6$ admits MST on a set of size $4$.
